# ASTRO: Teaching Language Models to Reason by Reflecting and Backtracking In-Context

Joongwon Kim Affiliation: AI at Meta Affiliation: University of
Washington    Anirudh Goyal Affiliation: AI at Meta    Liang Tan
Affiliation: AI at Meta    Hannaneh Hajishirzi Affiliation: University
of Washington    Srini Iyer Affiliation: AI at Meta    Tianlu Wang
Affiliation: AI at Meta

###### Abstract

We introduce Astro, the “Autoregressive Search-Taught Reasoner”, a
framework for training language models to reason like search algorithms,
explicitly leveraging self-reflection, backtracking, and exploration in
their outputs. Recently, training large language models (LLMs) via
reinforcement learning (RL) has led to the advent of reasoning models
with greatly enhanced reasoning capabilities. Open-source replications
of reasoning models, while successful, build upon models that already
exhibit strong reasoning capabilities along with search behavior
observed even before RL. As a result, it is yet unclear how to boost the
reasoning capabilities of other non-reasoner models including Llama 3.
Astro teaches such models to internalize structured search behavior
through a synthetic dataset derived from Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS)
over mathematical problem-solving trajectories. By converting search
traces into natural language chain-of-thoughts that capture both
successes and recoveries from failure, Astro bootstraps models with a
rich prior for exploration during RL. We finetune our models on these
search-derived traces and further improve performance via RL with
verifiable rewards. We apply Astro to the Llama 3 family of models and
achieve absolute performance gains of 16.0% on MATH-500, 26.9% on AMC
2023, and 20.0% on AIME 2024, especially improving upon challenging
problems that require iterative correction. Our results demonstrate that
search-inspired training offers a principled way to instill robust
reasoning capabilities into open LLMs.

## 1 Introduction

Training large language models (LLMs) via reinforcement learning (RL)
has greatly improved their reasoning capabilities, leading to the advent
of reasoning models such as OpenAI o1 ([OpenAI, 2024](#bib.bib21)),
DeepSeek-R1 ([DeepSeek-AI, 2025](#bib.bib3)) or Gemini 2.5 ([Google,
2025](#bib.bib5)). A prominent feature of reasoning models is their
ability to iteratively refine their outputs with a behavior similar to
search – a process which involves reflecting on their own outputs and
backtracking to a previous state ([Xiang et al., 2025](#bib.bib36)).
While open-source replications of reasoning models achieve notable
performance improvements, they rely on distillation from existing
reasoning models ([Li et al., 2025](#bib.bib13); [Muennighoff et al.,
2025](#bib.bib20)) or direct RL ([Hu et al., 2025](#bib.bib7); [Yu
et al., 2025](#bib.bib41)) from LLMs that (1) already contain reflective
behavior and strong reasoning capabilities ([Chang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib2); [Liu et al., 2025](#bib.bib16)), and (2) exhibit
spurious performance gains from incorrect or noisy reward signals during
RL ([Lv et al., 2025](#bib.bib19); [Shao et al., 2025](#bib.bib28)).
Hence it is unclear from a scientific perspective how reasoning models
can be built from other LLMs that do not exhibit the aforementioned
behavior, such as Llama 3 ([AI at Meta, 2024](#bib.bib1)).

![Refer to caption](2507.00417v1/astro_overview_v3.png)

Figure 2: An overview of Astro. Given a math reasoning problem, we first
perform Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) in a stepwise manner with
verifiable rewards and obtain a search tree where each node contains a
discrete reasoning step with its associated Q-value. We then linearize
the visited sequence of nodes, including intermediate nodes with
incorrect answers, into a solution that integrates backtracking and
self-reflection in natural language. Then, we perform supervised
fine-tuning (SFT) on the search-integrated solutions and bootstrap our
policy to perform autoregressive search. Finally, we further improve the
policy’s search and reasoning capabilities with reinforcement learning
(RL).

We introduce ASTRO, the “Autoregressive Search-Taught Reasoner”, a
framework that systematically infuses search-like behavior into language
models ab initio to improve their reasoning capabilities. The
fundamental principle guiding Astro is _search_, where our policy
explores the solution space by selecting actions, reflecting on its own
solution, and backtracking to a previous step if needed. Astro trains
language models to perform autoregressive search – instead of using
external search scaffolds such as beam search to solve reasoning
problems, Astro internalizes the search procedure and generates entire
search trajectories, including reflections and backtracks, in a single
inference pass. Models trained using Astro exhibit improved reasoning
abilities by frequently re-evaluating their solutions and backtracking
until they reach a final answer of high confidence. Moreover, such
models generate structured reasoning traces that can be mapped to a
directed graph with each vertex representing a discrete reasoning step,
allowing for a richer understanding of their reasoning processes.

Astro operates in three stages: (1) search trajectory generation, (2)
supervised fine-tuning and (3) reinforcement learning. We initially
bootstrap our models with search behavior by generating search
trajectories to be used for training data via procedure cloning ([Yang
et al., 2022](#bib.bib39); [Laskin et al., 2022](#bib.bib11)) – we
perform search with custom scaffolding over our language model policy to
explore over different solution trajectories for each math problem, and
we train our policy without using scaffolds at test time to predict the
entire sequence of actions, including intermediate actions that lead to
incorrect answers, that ultimately end with a successful terminal state.
Then, we further optimize our policy via RL to improve their reasoning
and search capabilities. Astro provides beneficial priors for RL during
its data generation stage by systematically injecting self-reflection
and backtracking patterns to the search traces via procedure cloning.

First, we generate synthetic data, also called the cold-start
data ([DeepSeek-AI, 2025](#bib.bib3); [Qwen, 2025](#bib.bib24)), to
instill autoregressive search priors to our models. To this end, we use
Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) to explore the solution space of
challenging math problems and build search trees with diverse reasoning
traces. We linearize each search tree into a sequence of nodes visited
during the search process, which we then convert into a natural language
chain-of-thought (CoT,  [Wei et al. (2022)](#bib.bib34)) that integrates
self-reflection and backtracking. Then, we sample about 36K high-quality
CoT solutions across three open-source math datasets.

We then perform supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to infuse autoregressive
search behavior into the Llama 3 family of models ([AI at Meta,
2024](#bib.bib1)). After fine-tuning for just one epoch, our SFT
checkpoint based on llama-3.1-70b-instruct achieves 69.6% on MATH-500,
55.0% on AMC 2023 and 13.3% on AIME 2024, and outperforms its
counterpart trained on the same set of problems but without search
priors. Our qualitative analyses show that even simply performing SFT
with high-quality search traces can infuse search capabilities,
including backtracking and self-reflection behavior, into a language
model.

Finally, we perform reinforcement learning (RL) on our models to further
improve their reasoning capabilities. Our training prompts are derived
from open-source math problems of moderate to high difficulties for our
policies. We use a modified form of Group Relative Policy Optimization
(GRPO,  [Shao et al. (2024)](#bib.bib29)) that is very similar to that
of Dr. GRPO ([Liu et al., 2025](#bib.bib16)) to update our policies.
After RL, our policy based on llama-3.1-70b-instruct achieves 81.8% in
MATH-500, 64.4% in AMC 2023 and 30.0% in AIME 2024 (pass@1). We show
that our model trained end-to-end using Astro outperforms its
counterpart similarly optimized with RL but initialized from a SFT
checkpoint trained without search priors – this demonstrates the
importance of leveraging self-reflection and backtracking as priors for
improving reasoning via RL. Our work provides a clear recipe for
improving the reasoning capabilities of language models by instilling
autoregressive search priors with SFT and leveraging such priors to
further improve the models via RL.

## 2 Search Trajectory Generation

Figure 3: Example of search trajectory generation via procedure cloning.
We use the policy to search through the solution space via MCTS and keep
track of terminal nodes with incorrect answers, as well as terminal
nodes with correct answers. Then, we linearize the search tree such that
it incorporates backtracking from the incorrect terminal node (Node 68)
to its greatest common ancestor (Node 16) with the correct terminal node
(Node 96). Finally, we rewrite the node sequence into a long
chain-of-thought, injecting self-reflection and backtracking phrases
into the CoTs.

Astro begins by generating a dataset of search traces, expressed as long
chain-of-thoughts ([Wei et al., 2022](#bib.bib34)) that encode
self-reflection and backtracking in natural language, via procedure
cloning. To this end, we first obtain search trees that explore a wide
solution space for each math problem using Monte Carlo Tree Search
(MCTS) in a stepwise manner, strategically balancing exploration and
exploitation with verifier-based rewards to obtain diverse and
high-quality solutions exploring different reasoning traces
(Section [2.2](#S2.SS2 "2.2 Monte Carlo Tree Search ‣ 2 Search Trajectory Generation ‣ ASTRO: Teaching Language Models to Reason by Reflecting and Backtracking In-Context")).

We then linearize the search trees into sequences of nodes that explore
various states, including intermediate nodes with incorrect answers,
until arriving at a high-quality solution leading to the correct answer
(Section [2.3](#S2.SS3 "2.3 Search Tree Linearization ‣ 2 Search Trajectory Generation ‣ ASTRO: Teaching Language Models to Reason by Reflecting and Backtracking In-Context")).
Finally, we translate each node sequence into a chain-of-thought that
integrates self-reflection and backtracking in natural language, and we
add each long chain-of-thought to our final dataset
(Section [2.4](#S2.SS4 "2.4 Procedure Cloning in Language ‣ 2 Search Trajectory Generation ‣ ASTRO: Teaching Language Models to Reason by Reflecting and Backtracking In-Context")).
The resulting dataset encodes beneficial self-reflection and
backtracking priors for training language models to perform
autoregressive search for solving challenging math problems via
supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning
(Section [3](#S3 "3 Learning to Search ‣ ASTRO: Teaching Language Models to Reason by Reflecting and Backtracking In-Context")).
Refer to
Figure [3](#S2.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 2 Search Trajectory Generation ‣ ASTRO: Teaching Language Models to Reason by Reflecting and Backtracking In-Context")
for a visual example of our search trajectory generation pipeline.

### 2.1 Problem Formulation and Overview

#### Problem formulation.

Our data generation setup is a Markov Decision Process (MDP) ([Puterman,
1994](#bib.bib22)), where the language model functions as the policy
$`\Pi_{\text{LM}}`$ and explores the solution space to the input
$`\mathbf{x}`$, while obtaining rewards in terminal states from a
verifier $`\mathcal{V}`$ based on the correct answer. Here we assume
that $`\Pi_{\text{LM}}`$ solves math problems in a stepwise manner,
where each step $`s_{t}`$ represents a sequence of tokens
$`y_{1}\cdots y_{\left|s_{t}\right|}`$ encapsulating a minimal unit of
reasoning required to solve $`\mathbf{x}`$. Then, each state $`S_{t}`$
represents a combination of the input prompt and the sequence of steps
generated by the policy, i.e. $`S_{t}=(\mathbf{x},s_{0},\cdots,s_{t})`$.
Meanwhile, the action $`a_{t+1}`$ represents the next step $`s_{t+1}`$
taken by $`\Pi_{\text{LM}}`$ to address $`\mathbf{x}`$. Refer to
Figure [3](#S2.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 2 Search Trajectory Generation ‣ ASTRO: Teaching Language Models to Reason by Reflecting and Backtracking In-Context")
for examples of the steps defined in our setup.

Given this setup, we teach a language model to predict a sequence of
states $`(S_{0}\cdots S_{\text{end}})`$ in response to $`\mathbf{x}`$
such that the states explore reasoning steps leading to correct and
incorrect answers, until the LM arrives at $`S_{\text{end}}`$ and
terminates its search by accepting the correct answer as its final
answer.

#### Overview.

We generate training data for Astro in three main stages outlined below:

1.  1.  For each $`\mathbf{x}`$ we generate a search tree $`T`$, where each
        node $`n_{i}`$ represents the state $`S_{i}`$ and each edge
        $`(n_{i},n_{j})`$ represents the action $`a_{j}`$, i.e. the next
        step $`s_{j}`$ taken from $`S_{i}`$ to $`S_{j}`$, using Monte Carlo
        Tree Search (MCTS) to explore the solution space based on
        verifier-based rewards from rollouts
        (Section [2.2](#S2.SS2 "2.2 Monte Carlo Tree Search ‣ 2 Search Trajectory Generation ‣ ASTRO: Teaching Language Models to Reason by Reflecting and Backtracking In-Context")).
2.  2.  We linearize $`T`$ into a sequence of nodes
        $`L=(n_{0},\cdots,n_{\text{end}})`$, a subsequence of the entire
        history of nodes visited by $`\Pi_{\text{LM}}`$ until arriving at
        $`n_{\text{end}}`$, the terminal node with the correct answer. Some
        adjacent pairs of nodes $`(n_{t},n_{t+1})`$ in $`L`$ are such that
        $`n_{t+1}`$ is an ancestor of $`n_{t}`$ in $`T`$, which corresponds
        to self-reflection and backtracking during the search procedure
        (Section [2.3](#S2.SS3 "2.3 Search Tree Linearization ‣ 2 Search Trajectory Generation ‣ ASTRO: Teaching Language Models to Reason by Reflecting and Backtracking In-Context")).
3.  3.  We translate $`L`$ into a chain-of-thought solution
        $`\mathbf{y}=(y_{0},\cdots,y_{\text{end}})`$ that integrates
        self-reflection and backtracking in natural language, and we add
        $`(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})`$ to our final dataset
        (Section [2.4](#S2.SS4 "2.4 Procedure Cloning in Language ‣ 2 Search Trajectory Generation ‣ ASTRO: Teaching Language Models to Reason by Reflecting and Backtracking In-Context")).

### 2.2 Monte Carlo Tree Search

We use our language model policy $`\Pi_{\text{LM}}`$ to obtain a search
tree with diverse solution traces to each input $`\mathbf{x}`$ by
running Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS). By using MCTS, we explore a
diverse solution space while balancing exploration and exploitation with
reliable guidance from reward signals obtained from full rollouts. Here,
we prompt $`\mathbf{x}`$ to elicit stepwise solutions from
$`\Pi_{\text{LM}}`$, and assign reward scores with our verifier
$`\mathcal{V}`$ to compare the predicted answer with the correct answer.

Monte Carlo Tree Search employs three main stages – selection, expansion
and backpropagation – to select promising next steps, expand the search
tree, and update the quality metric of each reasoning step.

#### Selection.

At state $`S_{t}`$ with $`k`$ actions generated by $`\Pi_{\text{LM}}`$
from $`S_{t}`$, we balance exploration and exploitation to select the
most promising node from which to further perform tree search. We use
the Predictor+Upper Confidence bounds applied to Trees (PUCT,  [Silver
et al. (2016)](#bib.bib30)) for selection to balance exploration and
exploitation during tree search. From any state $`S_{t}`$, given the
action index $`i\in\left[1...k\right]`$, the quality score of taking
action $`a_{i}`$ from state $`S_{t}`$ – $`Q(S_{t},a_{i})`$, the total
visit count of $`S_{t}`$ – $`N(S_{t})`$, and the visit count of taking
action $`a_{i}`$ from $`S_{t}`$ – $`N(S_{t},a_{i})`$, we perform
selection as:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
S_{t+1}^{*}=\argmax_{(S_{t+1}=S_{t}\rightarrow a_{i})}\left[Q(S_{t},a_{i})+c_{\text{puct}}\cdot\Pi_{\text{LM}}(a_{i}|S_{t})\frac{\sqrt{N(S_{t})}}{1+N(S_{t},a_{i})}\right]
``` |  | (1) |

#### Expansion.

From state $`S_{t}`$, $`\Pi_{\text{LM}}`$ takes $`\mathbf{x}`$ and the
sequence of steps $`(s_{0},\cdots,s_{t})`$ as the input, and first
samples $`k`$ actions which each correspond to the next step for solving
$`\mathbf{x}`$. For each action, we sample $`M`$ rollouts and score the
full solution using $`\mathcal{V}`$ to match the predicted answer with
the reference answer. Then, we average the scores across the rollouts
for each new action $`a_{i}`$ ($`i\in[1...k]`$) to compute the reward
scores for the new states. We add a new node $`n_{t+1}`$, associated
with each new state $`S_{t+1}`$, to $`T`$.

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
R(S_{t+1})=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{j\in[1...M]}\mathcal{V}(\Pi_{\text{LM},j}(S_{t+1}))
``` |  | (2) |

#### Backpropagation.

We backpropagate the reward scores obtained during expansion from the
leaf node to the root node to recursively update their Q-values. The
updates consist of (1) incrementing the visit count of each state
(Eq. [3](#S2.E3 "Equation 3 ‣ Backpropagation. ‣ 2.2 Monte Carlo Tree Search ‣ 2 Search Trajectory Generation ‣ ASTRO: Teaching Language Models to Reason by Reflecting and Backtracking In-Context")),
and (2) updating the Q-values of each (state, action) pair using the
Q-values and visit counts of the children nodes of
$`S_{t+1}=(S_{t},a)`$, along with the rollout-based reward score
$`R(S_{t+1})`$
(Eq. [4](#S2.E4 "Equation 4 ‣ Backpropagation. ‣ 2.2 Monte Carlo Tree Search ‣ 2 Search Trajectory Generation ‣ ASTRO: Teaching Language Models to Reason by Reflecting and Backtracking In-Context")).

|     |                     |     |     |
|-----|---------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       N(s_{t})=N(s_{t})+1
       ```                  |     | (3) |

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
Q(S_{t},a)=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{K}Q(S_{t+1},a_{i})\cdot N(S_{t+1},a_{i})+R(S_{t+1})}{\sum_{i=1}^{K}N(S_{t+1},a_{i})+1}
``` |  | (4) |

We repeat the procedure above for multiple iterations to explore the
solution space for each math problem and build the search trees. We use
llama-3.3-70b-instruct as our policy $`\Pi_{\text{LM}}`$ and generate
$`k=8`$ actions during each expansion step with $`M=16`$ rollouts,
$`c_{\text{puct}}=1.0`$, 32 iterations and maximum tree depth of 50.

### 2.3 Search Tree Linearization

Our goal is to use the search tree $`T`$ to obtain a sequence of states
$`(S_{0},\cdots,S_{\text{end}})`$ which represents a search procedure
exploring over correct and incorrect reasoning steps until arriving at
the correct answer to the input $`\mathbf{x}`$. To this end, we convert
$`T`$ into a linear sequence of nodes
$`L=(n_{0},\cdots,n_{\text{end}})`$.

In this process, we maintain the invariants that (1) the sequence ends
with a terminal node containing the correct answer, and (2) the
intermediate nodes may contain terminal nodes with incorrect answers,
but no two nodes in the same sequence may contain the same incorrect
answer. By maintaining these invariants, we ensure that our model learns
not to repeat the same incorrect answer or reasoning, and learns to
rectify its incorrect reasoning with a high-quality solution that leads
to the correct answer.

Our linearization procedure is detailed in
Algorithm [1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ 2.3 Search Tree Linearization ‣ 2 Search Trajectory Generation ‣ ASTRO: Teaching Language Models to Reason by Reflecting and Backtracking In-Context").
First, we perform depth-first search on $`T`$ to identify terminal nodes
with correct and incorrect answers, and we collect a subset of correct
terminal nodes with high-quality reasoning steps based on the policy’s
self-evaluation
(Appendix [A.1](#A1.SS1 "A.1 Self-Evaluation ‣ Appendix A Data Generation Details ‣ ASTRO: Teaching Language Models to Reason by Reflecting and Backtracking In-Context")).
We randomly sample a correct terminal node, and a subset of $`k`$
terminal nodes that contain distinct incorrect answers. Then, we iterate
through these terminal nodes, gather the sequence from the root node to
each terminal node, and sequentially merge the sequences. We thereby
obtain a linearized sequence $`L=(n_{0},\cdots,n_{\text{end}})`$ with
$`k`$ backtracking instances, where $`n_{\text{end}}`$ contains the
correct answer. We sample multiple node sequences from each search tree
by varying $`k\in\left[0,2\right]`$ and choosing different combinations
of incorrect answers, and we repeat this procedure over all search
trees.

Input: input $`\mathbf{x}`$, answer $`a`$, number of backtracks $`k`$,
policy $`\Pi`$, search tree $`T`$ with root node $`n_{0}`$

$`\Psi,\Lambda`$: set of terminal nodes with correct and incorrect
answers in $`T`$

$`\Psi^{\prime}`$: subset of $`\Psi`$ that contains high-quality
solutions

$`\Psi`$, $`\Lambda\leftarrow`$ DFS(root),
$`\Psi^{\prime}\leftarrow\left\{\right\}`$,
$`L\leftarrow\left[\ \right]`$

\# Collect all terminal nodes with high-quality, correct solutions

for $`n_{\psi}\in\Psi`$ do

  $`S\leftarrow`$ concat_steps_from_root($`n_{\psi}`$)

  if $`\Pi(\texttt{self\_eval\_prompt},S)`$ == 1 then
add($`\Psi^{\prime}`$, $`n_{\psi}`$)

end for

\# Sample a high-quality correct node, and a subset of $`k`$ nodes with
distinct incorrect answers

$`n_{\psi^{*}}\leftarrow`$ sample($`\Psi^{\prime}`$)

$`\Lambda_{k}\leftarrow`$ sample_with_unique_answers($`\Lambda`$, $`k`$)

\# Build the linearized sequence $`L`$ by tracking the $`k`$ incorrect
nodes and $`n_{\psi^{*}}`$

for $`n\in\Lambda_{k}\cup\left\{n_{\psi^{*}}\right\}`$ do

  $`l\leftarrow`$ gather_nodes_from_root($`n`$)

  $`L\leftarrow`$ merge_sequences($`L`$, $`l-L`$)

end for

Output: the linearized sequence of nodes $`L`$

Algorithm 1 Search Tree Linearization.

### 2.4 Procedure Cloning in Language

We convert $`L=(n_{0},\cdots,n_{\text{end}})`$ into a chain-of-thought
solution $`\mathbf{y}`$ by processing the nodes sequentially. Given the
node $`n_{t}`$ which contains a reasoning step $`s_{t}`$ and the
existing solution $`\mathbf{y}_{1:t-1}`$ at timestep $`t`$, we few-shot
prompt $`\Pi_{\text{LM}}`$ to generate $`y_{t}`$. We address two cases
(Appendix [A.2](#A1.SS2 "A.2 Chain-of-Thought Generation ‣ Appendix A Data Generation Details ‣ ASTRO: Teaching Language Models to Reason by Reflecting and Backtracking In-Context")):

Case 1: $`n_{t}`$ is a child of $`n_{t-1}`$. We simply convert the step
$`s_{t}`$ into $`y_{t}`$ which continues from $`\mathbf{y}_{1:t-1}`$.

Case 2: $`n_{t}`$ is an ancestor of $`n_{t-1}`$. In this case, we first
add a hard-coded self-reflection phrase But wait, are we solving the
problem correctly so far? Hmm..., followed by I’m not sure if we’re
solving the problem correctly so far. Then, we few-shot prompt
$`\Pi_{\text{LM}}`$ to generate a sentence that describes backtracking
(if $`n_{t}`$ is a non-root node – Let’s go back to where we ...) or
restart (if $`n_{t}`$ is a root node – Let’s restart our solution from
the beginning ...).

Moreover, between intermediate nodes with high Q-values and immediately
after the final node we inject the self-reflection phrase, followed by
Our solution seems to be correct so far., so that the model learns to
decide the correctness of its output after self-reflection, not before
self-reflection. In this way, our solution integrates self-reflection
followed by a continuation of the solution or backtracking to a previous
step. We repeat this procedure for all of our linearized node sequences.

## 3 Learning to Search

Using the search trajectories generated in chain-of-thought format
according to
Section [2](#S2 "2 Search Trajectory Generation ‣ ASTRO: Teaching Language Models to Reason by Reflecting and Backtracking In-Context"),
we train our models to perform autoregressive search in two stages. We
first use supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to infuse search priors including
self-reflection and backtracking into our models
(Section [3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 Supervised Fine-Tuning ‣ 3 Learning to Search ‣ ASTRO: Teaching Language Models to Reason by Reflecting and Backtracking In-Context")),
and then reinforcement learning (RL) to further improve their reasoning
capabilities
(Section [3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 Reinforcement Learning ‣ 3 Learning to Search ‣ ASTRO: Teaching Language Models to Reason by Reflecting and Backtracking In-Context")).

### 3.1 Supervised Fine-Tuning

We perform supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on a subset of the search
trajectories collected in
Section [2](#S2 "2 Search Trajectory Generation ‣ ASTRO: Teaching Language Models to Reason by Reflecting and Backtracking In-Context")
to instill self-reflection and backtracking priors into the Llama 3
family of models ([AI at Meta, 2024](#bib.bib1)). In this stage, we
focus on curating a relatively small amount of high-quality search
trajectories in order to carefully infuse our policy with helpful priors
to be exploited later during RL.

Dataset. We use three open math datasets of high school to competition
level: MATH-train ([Hendrycks et al., 2021](#bib.bib6)), and the
AMC/AIME and AoPS-forum subsets of NuminaMath ([Li et al.,
2024](#bib.bib14)).

| Dataset | \# problems | \# trajectories | \# backtracks | \# restarts |
|----|----|----|----|----|
| MATH-train | 5,838 | 12,536 | 3,817 | 4,191 |
| NuminaMath (AMC/AIME) | 1,599 | 5,758 | 3,268 | 1,341 |
| NuminaMath (AoPS Forum) | 4,702 | 17,773 | 11,608 | 2,636 |

Table 1: SFT dataset composition for our main Astro training run. Here,
\# problems refers to the number of unique problems, \# trajectories
refers to the total number of search trajectories, \# backtracks refers
to the number of backtracks to previous reasoning steps, and \# restarts
refers to the number of solution restarts in each training subset.

We build a total of 20.7K search trees and identify 14.0K search trees
with at least one high-quality, correct solution that can be linearized.
After linearization, we curate a total of 105K chain-of-thought
solutions. To construct our SFT dataset, for each math problem we sample
one direct solution without any backtracking ($`k=0)`$, and three search
solutions which reach the correct answer with at least one
self-reflection and backtracking instance ($`k\geq 1`$). Through this
process, we curate a total of 36.1K solutions across our datasets. Refer
to
Tables [1](#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 3.1 Supervised Fine-Tuning ‣ 3 Learning to Search ‣ ASTRO: Teaching Language Models to Reason by Reflecting and Backtracking In-Context")
and [5](#A2.T5 "Table 5 ‣ B.1 Training Dataset Details ‣ Appendix B Supervised Fine-Tuning Details ‣ ASTRO: Teaching Language Models to Reason by Reflecting and Backtracking In-Context")
for more information regarding the composition of our main SFT dataset.

Training. We perform SFT on llama-3.1-70b-instruct, and we simply train
on all tokens from each example without any masking. Refer to
Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Supervised Fine-Tuning Details ‣ ASTRO: Teaching Language Models to Reason by Reflecting and Backtracking In-Context")
for more details on our SFT procedure.

### 3.2 Reinforcement Learning

Based on our fine-tuned models that perform autoregressive search, we
further leverage the models’ search priors to improve their reasoning
capabilities through reinforcement learning (RL).

Dataset. We use open-source math datasets for our training prompts: AIME
1983-2023 which consist of AIME problems from the years 1983 to 2023,
MATH-4500 which is separated from the MATH-500 evaluation set, along
with MATH-train and the AMC/AIME and AoPS-forum subsets of NuminaMath.

| Dataset | \# problems total | pass rate avg. | \# problems solved | \# problems used |
|----|----|----|----|----|
| AIME 1983-2023 | 912 | 40.7% | 721 | 492 |
| MATH-4500 | 4,480 | 72.1% | 4,239 | 1,393 |
| MATH-train | 7,488 | 87.7% | 7,308 | 977 |
| NuminaMath (AMC/AIME) | 3,648 | 49.9% | 2,865 | 1,395 |
| NuminaMath (AoPS Forum) | 8,576 | 27.3% | 5,756 | 4,423 |

Table 2: RL dataset composition for our Astro-trained model based on
llama-3.1-70b-instruct. Here, \# problems total refers to the total
number of problems after string-based filtering for low-quality or
unverifiable problems, pass rate avg. refers to the mean pass rate
across $`N=64`$ outputs for all problems, \# problems solved refers to
the number of problems with a non-zero pass rate, and \# problems used
refers to the number of problems falling within the 1% to 75% pass rate
range for our SFT policy, which we use for our main RL experiment, in
each training subset.

To curate the final dataset, we use the model from
Section [3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 Supervised Fine-Tuning ‣ 3 Learning to Search ‣ ASTRO: Teaching Language Models to Reason by Reflecting and Backtracking In-Context")
to generate $`N=64`$ solutions for each problem in the datasets listed
above, and we compute the model’s pass rate, i.e. the fraction of
solutions that arrive at the correct answer. We curate problems where
the pass rate ranges from 1% (inclusive) to 75% (exclusive) to exclude
(1) problems that the policy is able to solve easily and (2) problems
that are too difficult for the policy to learn, and focus on problems of
moderate to high difficulty for the policy. Refer to
Table [2](#S3.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 3.2 Reinforcement Learning ‣ 3 Learning to Search ‣ ASTRO: Teaching Language Models to Reason by Reflecting and Backtracking In-Context")
for details of various statistics for our RL datasets.

Training. We train our models using Group Relative Policy Optimization
(GRPO, [Shao et al. (2024)](#bib.bib29)) while computing advantages
based on subtracting the prompt-level mean reward and removing the
standard deviation ([Liu et al., 2025](#bib.bib16)), and setting the KL
penalty to zero. Given our RL dataset $`\mathcal{D}`$ with training
examples $`(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})`$ where $`\mathbf{x}`$ is the input
prompt and $`\mathbf{y}`$ is the correct answer, a batch of solutions
$`\mathbf{S}`$ generated for each $`\mathbf{x}`$, the verifier
$`\mathcal{V}`$ which assigns a binary correctness score to each
solution $`\mathbf{s}\in\mathbf{S}`$ based on $`\mathbf{y}`$, as well as
our policy $`\pi_{\theta}`$, we optimize its parameters $`\theta`$ such
that the following holds:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\max_{\theta}\mathbb{E}_{(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})\sim\mathcal{D}}\left[\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{s}\in\mathbf{S}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|\mathbf{x})}\left[\mathcal{V}(\mathbf{s},\mathbf{y})-\frac{1}{\|\mathbf{S}\|}\sum_{\mathbf{s^{\prime}}\in\mathbf{S}}\mathcal{V}(\mathbf{s^{\prime}},\mathbf{y})\right]\right]
``` |  | (5) |

By using this objective, we optimize the policy to generate solution
trajectories that produce correct answers by leveraging the
self-reflection and backtracking priors to reconsider incorrect
solutions or correct-but-uncertain solutions and finally arrive at
high-confidence solutions with correct answers.

## 4 Experiments and Results

### 4.1 Experimental Setup

Training. We train our models with datasets summarized in
Sections [3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 Supervised Fine-Tuning ‣ 3 Learning to Search ‣ ASTRO: Teaching Language Models to Reason by Reflecting and Backtracking In-Context")
and [3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 Reinforcement Learning ‣ 3 Learning to Search ‣ ASTRO: Teaching Language Models to Reason by Reflecting and Backtracking In-Context")
for SFT and RL. For our SFT experiments, we fine-tune
llama-3.1-70b-instruct on our synthetic dataset with 36.1K search
trajectories for 1 epoch only, in order to prevent overfitting to the
SFT dataset. For our RL experiments, we further optimize the checkpoints
we obtain from the SFT stage using the objective presented in
Equation [5](#S3.E5 "Equation 5 ‣ 3.2 Reinforcement Learning ‣ 3 Learning to Search ‣ ASTRO: Teaching Language Models to Reason by Reflecting and Backtracking In-Context").
Refer to
Appendix [B.2](#A2.SS2 "B.2 Training Hyperparameters ‣ Appendix B Supervised Fine-Tuning Details ‣ ASTRO: Teaching Language Models to Reason by Reflecting and Backtracking In-Context")
and [C.1](#A3.SS1 "C.1 Training Hyperparameters ‣ Appendix C Reinforcement Learning Details ‣ ASTRO: Teaching Language Models to Reason by Reflecting and Backtracking In-Context")
for more details on our training hyperparameters.

Evaluation. We evaluate our models on three widely-used math evaluation
benchmarks – MATH-500 ([Hendrycks et al., 2021](#bib.bib6)), AMC
(American Mathematics Competition) 2023 and AIME (American Invitational
Mathematics Examination) 2024. Due to the lower number of examples
present in the AMC 2023 and AIME 2024 benchmarks, we compute the pass@1
score by averaging across $`N=16`$ generations. We also compute the
maj@8 score by sampling a random subset of eight outputs over ten
simulations and averaging the scores obtained for the majority answers
across the ten simulations.

Baselines. Our baselines include llama-3.1-70b-instruct, which employs
SFT followed by Direct Preference Optimization (DPO,  [Rafailov et al.
(2023)](#bib.bib25)) for post-training and llama-3.3-70b-instruct, which
is further trained via online RL. Moreover, we compare with two methods
based on RL or self-correction that improve mathematical reasoning for
Llama 3 models: Step-KTO([Lin et al., 2025](#bib.bib15)) , and a
baseline that learns to self-correct and verify in-context with traces
obtained via Pair-SFT ([Welleck et al., 2023](#bib.bib35)) and is
further improved with RL, which we call ”spontaneous self-correction” or
SPOC.

| Checkpoint                        | MATH-500 | AMC 2023 |       | AIME 2024 |       |
|-----------------------------------|----------|----------|-------|-----------|-------|
|                                   | pass@1   | pass@1   | maj@8 | pass@1    | maj@8 |
| Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct            | 65.8     | 37.5     | 47.5  | 10.0      | 16.7  |
| Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct            | 75.8     | 57.5     | 60.0  | 26.7      | 30.0  |
| Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct (SPOC)     | 77.4     | 52.5     | \-    | 23.3      | \-    |
| Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct (Step-KTO) | 76.2     | 60.0     | 67.5  | 16.7      | 20.0  |
| Llama-3.1-70B-ASTRO-SFT           | 69.6     | 51.9     | 63.0  | 16.3      | 24.7  |
| Llama-3.1-70B-ASTRO-RL            | 81.8     | 64.4     | 68.8  | 30.0      | 32.0  |
| Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct (SPOC)     | 77.8     | 70.0     | \-    | 23.3      | \-    |
| Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct (Step-KTO) | 79.6     | 70.0     | 75.0  | 30.0      | 33.3  |

Table 3: Main experiment results. Llama-3.1-70B-ASTRO-SFT outperforms
llama-3.1-70b-instruct with high-quality search trajectories obtained
via procedure cloning. Llama-3.1-70B-ASTRO-RL outperforms
llama-3.3-70b-instruct, as well as SPOC and Step-KTO based on
llama-3.1-70b-instruct, and even outperforms or performs on par with
SPOC and Step-KTO based on llama-3.3-70b-instruct on MATH-500 and AIME
2024, respectively.²² 2 We do not present results for Astro with
llama-3.3-70b-instruct due to the unstable behavior of the model. More
specifically, we observe that its generated CoT length explodes after
some number of steps, causing a collapse in its benchmark performance.
Note that our pass@1 scores for AMC 2023 and AIME 2024 evaluations are
averaged over 16 different runs, while the baseline scores are not.

Figure 4: Training curves detailing how Llama-3.1-70B-ASTRO-RL behaves

### 4.2 Main Results

Table [2](#footnote2 "Footnote 2 ‣ Table 3 ‣ 4.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ ASTRO: Teaching Language Models to Reason by Reflecting and Backtracking In-Context")
presents the results of applying Astro to llama-3.1-70b-instruct. Our
initial checkpoint trained on our search trajectories with SFT, named
Llama-3.1-70B-ASTRO-SFT, improves over llama-3.1-70b-instruct across all
benchmarks. Meanwhile, our llama-3.1-70b-instruct trained end-to-end via
Astro with RL, which we name Llama-3.1-70B-ASTRO-RL, outperforms
llama-3.3-70b-instruct as well as SPOC and Step-KTO applied to
llama-3.1-70b-instruct while outperforming and performing on par with
SPOC and Step-KTO applied to llama-3.3-70b-instruct on MATH-500 and AIME
2024, respectively.

Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ ASTRO: Teaching Language Models to Reason by Reflecting and Backtracking In-Context")
visualizes how the generation length of Llama-3.1-70B-ASTRO-RL, as well
as reward scores assigned to the model, evolve while running RL. We
observe that the policy’s CoT generation length initially increases
quite noticeably, similar to training runs for other reasoning
models ([DeepSeek-AI, 2025](#bib.bib3); [Kimi, 2025](#bib.bib8)), and
then grows slowly after this initial phase. The reward scores increase
monotonically overall, indicating that the policy learns to solve more
math problems correctly. Meanwhile,
Figure [5](#S4.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 4.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ ASTRO: Teaching Language Models to Reason by Reflecting and Backtracking In-Context")
visualizes how the performance of Llama-3.1-70B-ASTRO-RL on MATH-500,
AMC 2023 and AIME 2024 evolves during RL. We observe that the evaluation
metrics continue to increase steadily across all three benchmarks with
more RL. Refer to
Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E Qualitative Examples ‣ ASTRO: Teaching Language Models to Reason by Reflecting and Backtracking In-Context")
for examples of chain-of-thoughts generated by models trained with Astro
after SFT and RL.

| Checkpoint               | MATH-500 | AMC 2023 |       | AIME 2024 |       |
|--------------------------|----------|----------|-------|-----------|-------|
|                          | pass@1   | pass@1   | maj@8 | pass@1    | maj@8 |
| Llama-3.1-70B-Direct-SFT | 65.8     | 45.2     | 58.0  | 16.7      | 23.3  |
| Llama-3.1-70B-ASTRO-SFT  | 69.6     | 51.9     | 63.0  | 13.3      | 16.7  |
| Llama-3.1-70B-Direct-RL  | 79.8     | 60.5     | 67.8  | 27.1      | 30.3  |
| Llama-3.1-70B-ASTRO-RL   | 81.8     | 64.4     | 68.8  | 30.0      | 32.0  |

Table 4: Results of our experiment which compares training on solutions
without self-reflection and backtracking priors (Direct) vs. training on
solutions with self-reflection and backtracking priors (Astro) completed
after SFT (Top) and RL (Bottom), based on the same set of input math
problems and CoT solutions curated from the same search trees. Models
trained with Astro outperform their counterparts trained without
explicit search priors across all benchmarks.

![Refer to caption](2507.00417v1/astro_direct_ablation_main_v3.png)

Figure 7: RL training curves for our no-search baseline vs. Astro,
averaged over the three evaluation benchmarks. The difference between

for RL.

### 4.3 Impact of the Search Prior

While the performance of Astro-trained models demonstrate notable
performance gains even with a relatively small dataset, such
improvements to the model’s reasoning capabilities can be attributed to
both (1) the self-reflection and backtracking priors infused during
Astro, and (2) the high-quality chain-of-thoughts curated from the
search trees
(Section [2.2](#S2.SS2 "2.2 Monte Carlo Tree Search ‣ 2 Search Trajectory Generation ‣ ASTRO: Teaching Language Models to Reason by Reflecting and Backtracking In-Context")).
Therefore we seek to isolate and verify the importance of the search
prior, a core component of Astro that shapes the behavior of the policy
during SFT and RL.

Search behavior during RL. We seek to better understand the role of the
self-reflection and backtracking priors used in Astro.
Figure [6](#S4.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ 4.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ ASTRO: Teaching Language Models to Reason by Reflecting and Backtracking In-Context")
(Top) shows that our policy learns to perform more self-reflections and
backtracks as RL progresses, while
Figure [6](#S4.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ 4.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ ASTRO: Teaching Language Models to Reason by Reflecting and Backtracking In-Context")
(Bottom) shows that the number of backtracks employed at test-time is
highly correlated with evaluation performance during RL, with the
Pearson’s coefficient scoring 0.816, 0.851 and 0.854 across the three
benchmarks, respectively. These results strongly indicate that learning
to self-reflect and backtrack more frequently helps the model to solve
challenging math problems. Refer to
Appendix [C.4](#A3.SS4 "C.4 Test-time scaling Analysis ‣ Appendix C Reinforcement Learning Details ‣ ASTRO: Teaching Language Models to Reason by Reflecting and Backtracking In-Context")
for a similar analysis on the generation length.

Training without search priors. To isolate the impact of search priors
on Astro, we perform a control experiment where we begin with
llama-3.1-70b-instruct and the same problem set used for finetuning
Llama-3.1-70B-ASTRO-SFT with the same number of examples, as well as the
CoT solutions curated from the same search trees, but only using direct
solutions that do not contain any self-reflection or backtracking
priors. We name the resulting checkpoint Llama-3.1-70B-Direct-SFT.
Afterwards, we use the same set of prompts used for training
Llama-3.1-70B-ASTRO-RL and perform RL on Llama-3.1-70B-Direct-SFT for
the same number of training steps to obtain Llama-3.1-70B-Direct-RL. We
run RL on a policy without the search priors used in Astro to quantify
their importance for RL. Refer to
Appendix [D](#A4 "Appendix D Details for Llama-3.1-70B-Direct-RL ‣ ASTRO: Teaching Language Models to Reason by Reflecting and Backtracking In-Context")
for more details on this experiment.

Figure 8: Example of Llama-3.1-70B-ASTRO-RL solving a problem from AMC
2023. (Left) The model generates a long CoT that contains
self-reflections (black) and backtracking (blue) and explores the
solution space, backtracking from reasoning traces with the incorrect
answer (red) until arriving at a reasoning trace with the correct answer
(green). (Right) The CoT is mapped to a directed graph where its nodes
represent discrete reasoning steps. The arrows indicate the search
process, with the blue arrows for backtracking and the dotted arrows for
the omitted intermediate steps.

Table [4](#S4.T4 "Table 4 ‣ 4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ ASTRO: Teaching Language Models to Reason by Reflecting and Backtracking In-Context")
shows the results of our experiments. We initially find that
Llama-3.1-70B-ASTRO-SFT outperforms Llama-3.1-70B-Direct-SFT in MATH-500
and AMC 2023, but slightly underperforms in AIME 2024. After RL,
Llama-3.1-70B-Direct-RL achieves gains across our benchmarks, but even
its best checkpoint underperforms Llama-3.1-70B-ASTRO-RL across all
benchmarks by nontrivial margins.
Figure [7](#S4.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ 4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ ASTRO: Teaching Language Models to Reason by Reflecting and Backtracking In-Context")
further corroborates our results by showcasing the averaged evaluation
metrics across our three benchmarks over the entire RL training for both
models, demonstrating how our policy initialized with search priors
(Astro) exhibit better training efficacy and upper bound during RL
compared to our policy initialized without search priors (Direct). By
showing the limitations of our policy trained on solutions curated from
identical sources but without the self-reflection and backtracking
priors, we demonstrate the importance of the search priors used in
Astro.

Qualitative Example. The benefit of using search priors can also be
observed using qualitative examples. Refer to
Figure [8](#S4.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ 4.3 Impact of the Search Prior ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ ASTRO: Teaching Language Models to Reason by Reflecting and Backtracking In-Context")
for an example output from Llama-3.1-70B-ASTRO-RL. Our model
intermittently reflects over its own solution, backtracks from uncertain
outputs to a previous reasoning step, and repeats this procedure,
exploring over the solution space until arriving at a final answer. Note
how every CoT generated by our model trained with Astro can be mapped to
a directed graph with each node representing a discrete reasoning step,
allowing for easier visualization and state-tracking of the model’s
reasoning process. Refer to
Appendix [E.2](#A5.SS2 "E.2 ASTRO-RL ‣ Appendix E Qualitative Examples ‣ ASTRO: Teaching Language Models to Reason by Reflecting and Backtracking In-Context")
for more examples of search trajectories generated by
Llama-3.1-70B-ASTRO-RL.

## 5 Related Work

Self-correction for reasoning. [Setlur et al. (2024)](#bib.bib26) find
that training models on per-step negative responses can help to unlearn
spurious correlations in the positive data. Similarly, [Ye et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib40) show that adding pretraining data with erroneous
solution steps immediately followed by their corrections helps language
models achieve higher accuracies on a synthetic math dataset. [Qu et al.
(2024)](#bib.bib23) show that language models can be trained to improve
their solutions to math problems in-context via iterative fine-tuning,
and [Kumar et al. (2025)](#bib.bib9) develop a multi-turn online RL
method that improves their self-correction abilities using entirely
self-generated data and also show that training language models to
perform self-correction can improve their mathematical reasoning
capabilities. [Snell et al. (2024)](#bib.bib31) similarly report that
scaling the number of revisions performed in-context for math problems
improves the accuracy of the final predicted answers.

Learning to search for reasoning. [Laskin et al. (2022)](#bib.bib11)
propose algorithm distillation, which distills RL algorithms into neural
networks in an autoregressive manner by training on their learning
histories, and their resulting policy improves in-context without
gradient updates. Also, [Yang et al. (2022)](#bib.bib39) introduce
procedure cloning, which learns from series of expert computations and
generalizes better to unseen environments including ones for maze
navigation, simulated robotic manipulation and game-playing. [Lehnert
et al. (2024)](#bib.bib12) introduce Searchformer, a transformer trained
to predict the sequences of the A\* search algorithm in-context while
solving the Sokoban puzzle. Meanwhile, [Gandhi et al. (2024)](#bib.bib4)
train language models to imitate different search strategies such as BFS
or DFS for addressing the Countdown task. [Xiang et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib36) propose applying procedure cloning to search traces
of language models operated via A\* or MCTS to improve their math
reasoning abilities, showcasing several proof-of-concept examples.
Recently, [Setlur et al. (2025)](#bib.bib27) propose a new RL recipe
that encourages the policy to perform in-context exploration and
similarly observe that this behavior improves the math capabilities of
Qwen3-1.7B ([Qwen, 2025](#bib.bib24)).

Reinforcement learning for reasoning. [Luo et al. (2025)](#bib.bib18);
[Wang et al. (2024)](#bib.bib32); [Shao et al. (2024)](#bib.bib29) show
that training language models with with on-policy RL involving reward
models improves the policies’ math reasoning abilities, and  [Yang
et al. (2024b)](#bib.bib38); [Lambert et al. (2024)](#bib.bib10) propose
using RL with verifiable rewards instead of model-generated rewards for
more stable reward assignment. Shortly after, [DeepSeek-AI
(2025)](#bib.bib3); [Kimi (2025)](#bib.bib8) use RL with verifiable
rewards to train language models to generate long CoTs with cognitive
behavior such as self-correction, which greatly improves the reasoning
capabilities of the language models. More recently, [Hu et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib7); [Yu et al. (2025)](#bib.bib41); [Liu et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib16) similarly perform RL with verifiable rewards on the
Qwen base models ([Yang et al., 2024a](#bib.bib37); [Yang et al.,
2024b](#bib.bib38)) and achieve significant improvements in their
reasoning capabilities.

## 6 Conclusion

We introduce Astro, a new framework for training LLMs to reason like
search algorithms. Astro operates in three stages: (1) data generation
(2) supervised fine-tuning, and (3) reinforcement learning. We first
build search trees using Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS), linearize the
trees into node sequences encoding the search procedure, and translate
the node sequences into long CoTs that integrate self-reflection and
backtracking in natural language. Then, we fine-tune our language model
on the long CoTs via SFT to instill the search priors and further
improve their reasoning capabilities via RL. Our model trained using
Astro learns to perform self-reflections and backtracking in-context,
and outperforms other baselines applying different post-training
techniques on the Llama 3 family of models. Moreover, our model learns
to self-reflect and backtrack more frequently during RL while generating
longer chain-of-thoughts, and we verify that the search priors used in
Astro contribute to improving our model’s reasoning capabilities. Our
framework offers a systematic recipe to instill robust reasoning
capabilities into open-source LLMs.

## Appendix A Data Generation Details

### A.1 Self-Evaluation

We provide more details regarding the self-evaluation used during
linearization
(Section [2.3](#S2.SS3 "2.3 Search Tree Linearization ‣ 2 Search Trajectory Generation ‣ ASTRO: Teaching Language Models to Reason by Reflecting and Backtracking In-Context"))
of our search trees. We prompt the policy $`\Pi_{\text{LM}}`$ to provide
a reason for whether the given solution contains valid reasoning or not
by first “thinking” whether the solution skips complicated math
operations, overlooks important casework or performs a lucky guess to
arrive at the answer. Then, the policy returns a binary answer of “yes”
or “no” to conclude whether the reasoning is valid or not. We use a
few-shot prompt, presented below, to instruct the policy to follow the
exact demonstrated format for returning validation thoughts followed by
a “yes” or “no” answer. Moreover, we generate $`N=8`$ self-evaluations
per solution and employ a form of self-consistency \[[Wang et al.,
2023](#bib.bib33)\] to obtain multiple votes on the quality of the
solution to increase the reliability of our self-evaluation, and we
obtain an averaged quality score $`s_{i}`$ for the solution $`S_{i}`$.

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
s_{i}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\mathbbm{1}\left[\Pi_{\text{LM}}(S_{i})=\text{yes}\right]
``` |  |

We only consider solutions with score $`s_{i}=1`$, which imply unanimous
agreement between the $`N=8`$ self-evaluations, to be “high-quality”
solutions. We present our few-shot self-evaluation prompt below.

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

Given the following math problem and the solution, decide whether the
final answer to the problem was obtained via correct reasoning, or if
the final answer was obtained with insufficient reasoning or a lucky
guess. Think before arriving at the final answer, which must be answered
"yes" for correct reasoning, and "no" for incorrect reasoning.

Examples of answers obtained via incorrect reasoning include:

- The solution presents a complicated mathematical operation (e.g.,
numerical methods for integration) that must be completed to solve the
problem and returns the answer without any details on how the operation
was performed to arrive at the answer.

- The solution presents casework for arriving at the final answer (case
1, case 2, ...) but returns the final answer after considering only a
subset of the cases without explaining why the other cases were not
considered.

- The solution performs a random guess for the final answer without any
justified explanation for why that guess was made. Educated guesses are
okay.

Below are a few examples of math problems and their solutions, the
thinking process for determining why the reasoning is correct or
incorrect, and the final decision for whether the reasonign is correct
or not.

---

Problem: Let f(x)=\|x-p\|+\|x-15\|+\|x-p-15\| , where 0 \< p \< 15 .
Determine the minimum value taken by f(x) for x in the interval p \\leq
x\\leq15.

Solution:

\## Step 1: Understanding the given function

The given function is f(x) = \|x-p\| + \|x-15\| + \|x-p-15\|, where 0 \<
p \< 15. We need to find the minimum value of f(x) for x in the interval
p \\leq x \\leq 15.

\## Step 2: Analyzing the behavior of f(x) in the interval p \\leq x
\\leq 15

For x in the interval p \\leq x \\leq 15, we observe the behavior of
each absolute value term. Since x \\geq p, \|x-p\| = x-p. For \|x-15\|,
since x \\leq 15, \|x-15\| = 15-x. The term \|x-p-15\| requires closer
examination because its behavior changes based on the value of x
relative to p+15. However, given that x \\leq 15 and p \< 15, x will
always be less than or equal to 15, and thus \|x-p-15\| = p+15-x for x
in the given interval.

\## Step 3: Simplifying the function for the given interval

Substituting the simplified expressions back into f(x) gives us f(x) =
(x-p) + (15-x) + (p+15-x). Simplifying this, f(x) = x - p + 15 - x + p +
15 - x = 30 - x.

\## Step 4: Finding the minimum value of f(x) in the interval

The function f(x) = 30 - x is a linear function with a negative slope,
meaning its minimum value in the interval p \\leq x \\leq 15 will occur
at the maximum value of x in that interval, which is x = 15.
Substituting x = 15 into f(x), we find f(15) = 30 - 15 = 15.

The final answer is: \\boxed{15}.

Correctness thoughts: The solution correctly considers the range of p,
given as p \\leq x\\leq15, and uses this information to remove the
absolute value operators and simplify the given function. Then, it
correctly reasons that the function f(x) = 30 - x is decreasing in the
interval p \\leq x\\leq15 and therefore the minimum value must happen at
x = 15, which is 30 - 15 = 15.

Is correct reasoning: yes

Problem: A machine-shop cutting tool has the shape of a notched circle,
as shown. The radius of the circle is \\sqrt{50} cm, the length of AB is
6 cm and that of BC is 2 cm. The angle ABC is a right angle. Find the
square of the distance (in centimeters) from B to the center of the
circle. \[asy\] size(150); defaultpen(linewidth(0.6)+fontsize(11)); real
r=10; pair O=(0,0), A=r\*dir(45),B=(A.x,A.y-r); path P=circle(O,r); pair
C=intersectionpoint(B--(B.x+r,B.y),P); // Drawing arc instead of full
circle //draw(P); draw(arc(O, r, degrees(A), degrees(C)));
draw(C--B--A--B); dot(A); dot(B); dot(C); label("A",A,NE);
label("B",B,S); label("C",C,SE); \[/asy\]

Solution:

\## Step 1: To solve this problem, we need to find the square of the
distance from point B to the center of the circle.

The problem involves a notched circle with a radius of \\sqrt{50} cm and
points A, B, and C as described.

\## Step 2: Let’s denote the center of the circle as O and the foot of
the altitude from O to AB as D.

We need to find the square of the distance from B to the center of the
circle, which is OB^2.

\## Step 3: Using the Pythagorean theorem, we can express the
relationship between the lengths of the sides of triangle OAB.

By applying the Pythagorean theorem to triangle OAB, we get OA^2 =
OB^2 + AB^2. Substituting the given values, we have 50 = OB^2 + 36.

\## Step 4: Similarly, for triangle OBC, we can use the Pythagorean
theorem to relate the lengths of its sides.

Applying the Pythagorean theorem to triangle OBC, we get OC^2 = OB^2 +
BC^2. Substituting the given values, we have 50 = OB^2 + 4.

\## Step 5: By solving the equations from steps 3 and 4, we can find the
value of OB^2.

From step 4, we can express OB^2 as 50 - 4 = 46. This value represents
the square of the distance from point B to the center of the circle.

The final answer is: \\boxed{26}.

Correctness thoughts: The problem is asking for OB^2 according to our
notation, and Step 5 indicates that OB^2 is equal to 46. However, the
final answer is 26 without any explanation as to why it returned 26
instead of 46.

### A.2 Chain-of-Thought Generation

We provide more details for how we convert the linearized sequence of
nodes into a natural language CoT that integrates self-reflection and
backtracking
(Section [2.4](#S2.SS4 "2.4 Procedure Cloning in Language ‣ 2 Search Trajectory Generation ‣ ASTRO: Teaching Language Models to Reason by Reflecting and Backtracking In-Context")).
As we iterate over the sequence of nodes, for each node $`n_{t}`$ at
timestep $`t`$ we sample $`\Pi_{\text{LM}}`$ with few-shot prompts
conditioned upon the CoT generated so far ($`\mathbf{y}_{1\dots t-1}`$),
where (a) case 1 – $`n_{t}`$ is a descendant of $`n_{t-1}`$: the
few-shot prompt involves directly rewriting $`s_{t}`$ into a CoT format,
and (b) case 2 – $`n_{t}`$ is an ancestor of $`n_{t-1}`$: the few-shot
prompt involves writing a phrase the backtracks from $`n_{t-1}`$ to
$`n_{t}`$. Below we present the few-shot prompts for rewriting and
backtracking.

## Appendix B Supervised Fine-Tuning Details

### B.1 Training Dataset Details

We present a more detailed breakdown of the statistics during the
generation of our supervised fine-tuning (SFT) dataset composed of
long-CoT search trajectories
(Section [3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 Supervised Fine-Tuning ‣ 3 Learning to Search ‣ ASTRO: Teaching Language Models to Reason by Reflecting and Backtracking In-Context")).
Table [5](#A2.T5 "Table 5 ‣ B.1 Training Dataset Details ‣ Appendix B Supervised Fine-Tuning Details ‣ ASTRO: Teaching Language Models to Reason by Reflecting and Backtracking In-Context")
presents a detailed breakdown of the statistics during the intermediate
stages of our data curation, as presented in
Table [1](#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 3.1 Supervised Fine-Tuning ‣ 3 Learning to Search ‣ ASTRO: Teaching Language Models to Reason by Reflecting and Backtracking In-Context")
in the main paper, across the three math dataset sources used for
instilling search behaviors during the initial stages of Astro.

| Dataset | \# trees | \# valid trees | \# solutions | \# direct | \# search |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|
| MATH-train | 6,912 | 6,118 | 12,536 | 5,838 | 6,698 |
| NuminaMath (AMC/AIME) | 2,480 | 1,812 | 5,758 | 1,746 | 4,012 |
| NuminaMath (AoPS Forum) | 11,329 | 6,069 | 17,773 | 4,706 | 13,067 |

Table 5: Detailed statistics of our data curation procedure in Astro
resulting in our main SFT dataset. Here, \# trees refers to the number
of search trees from the initial set of problems, \# valid trees refers
to the number of search trees with at least one high-quality solution
ending with the correct answer, \# solutions refers to the number of
long chain-of-thought solutions curated from the valid search trees, \#
direct refers to the number of solutions without self-reflection or
backtracking, and \# search refers to the number of solutions with
self-reflection and backtracking.

### B.2 Training Hyperparameters

We train our model for one epoch only to provide a better initialization
for the RL stage. We use the AdamW  \[[Loshchilov and Hutter,
2019](#bib.bib17)\] optimizer with an initial learning rate of 3e-6 and
a cosine scheduler, and we set the maximum sequence length to be 8,192
tokens.

### B.3 Hardware Specifications

We train our 70B models across 8 GPU nodes with each node consisting of
8 NVIDIA H100 GPUs. Under this setup, training for one epoch on our SFT
dataset takes approximately 40 minutes.

## Appendix C Reinforcement Learning Details

### C.1 Training Hyperparameters

For reinforcement learning
(Section [3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 Reinforcement Learning ‣ 3 Learning to Search ‣ ASTRO: Teaching Language Models to Reason by Reflecting and Backtracking In-Context")),
we use a constant learning rate of 2e-7, four rollouts per prompt for
advantage estimation, a batch size of 256 for every step, gradient
accumulation step of 1, maximum sequence length of 15,360 tokens, a
temperature of 1.0, and 80 warmup steps.

### C.2 Hardware Specifications

We run RL with our 70B models across 32 GPU nodes with each node
consisting of 8 NVIDIA H100 GPUs. We use 128 GPUs for training and 128
GPUs for inference, respectively. Each of our RL training runs takes
about 10 days to complete.

### C.3 Reward Scores by Dataset

We visualize the evolution of reward scores (recall
Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ ASTRO: Teaching Language Models to Reason by Reflecting and Backtracking In-Context"))
on a per-dataset basis for training Llama-3.1-70B-ASTRO-RL, which
consist of AIME problems from the years 1983 to 2023, MATH-4500 which is
separated from the MATH-500 evaluation set, along with MATH-train and
the AMC/AIME and AoPS-forum subsets of NuminaMath \[[Li et al.,
2024](#bib.bib14)\]. Refer to
Figures [10](#A2.F10 "Figure 10 ‣ B.4 SFT Visualizations ‣ Appendix B Supervised Fine-Tuning Details ‣ ASTRO: Teaching Language Models to Reason by Reflecting and Backtracking In-Context"), [11](#A2.F11 "Figure 11 ‣ B.4 SFT Visualizations ‣ Appendix B Supervised Fine-Tuning Details ‣ ASTRO: Teaching Language Models to Reason by Reflecting and Backtracking In-Context"), [12](#A2.F12 "Figure 12 ‣ B.4 SFT Visualizations ‣ Appendix B Supervised Fine-Tuning Details ‣ ASTRO: Teaching Language Models to Reason by Reflecting and Backtracking In-Context"), [13](#A2.F13 "Figure 13 ‣ B.4 SFT Visualizations ‣ Appendix B Supervised Fine-Tuning Details ‣ ASTRO: Teaching Language Models to Reason by Reflecting and Backtracking In-Context"), [14](#A2.F14 "Figure 14 ‣ B.4 SFT Visualizations ‣ Appendix B Supervised Fine-Tuning Details ‣ ASTRO: Teaching Language Models to Reason by Reflecting and Backtracking In-Context")
and [15](#A2.F15 "Figure 15 ‣ B.4 SFT Visualizations ‣ Appendix B Supervised Fine-Tuning Details ‣ ASTRO: Teaching Language Models to Reason by Reflecting and Backtracking In-Context")
for the overall reward scores as well as the reward scores on each
training subset, in order.

### C.4 Test-time scaling Analysis

#### Number of generated tokens during evaluation.

In
Figure [16](#A3.F16 "Figure 16 ‣ Number of generated tokens during evaluation. ‣ C.4 Test-time scaling Analysis ‣ Appendix C Reinforcement Learning Details ‣ ASTRO: Teaching Language Models to Reason by Reflecting and Backtracking In-Context"),
we show the number of tokens generated by Llama-3.1-70B-ASTRO-RL during
RL. The policy initially generates a steeply increasing number of
tokens, and this rate decreases afterwards but keeps a steady pace,
similar to the number of backtracks in
Figure [5](#S4.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 4.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ ASTRO: Teaching Language Models to Reason by Reflecting and Backtracking In-Context").

![Refer to caption](2507.00417v1/astro_num_generated_tokens_v2.png)

Figure 16: Number of generated tokens on the MATH-500, AMC 2023 and AIME
2024 benchmarks while training Llama-3.1-70B-ASTRO-RL. The number of
generated tokens initially increases rapidly as the model learns to
perform more self-reflections and backtracks (see
Figure [5](#S4.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 4.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ ASTRO: Teaching Language Models to Reason by Reflecting and Backtracking In-Context")),
and then increases more slowly but steadily afterwards.

#### Relationship with Evaluation Metrics

We plot the relationship between the number of tokens generated during
evaluation and the model’s performance. We find a strong correlation
with a Pearson’s coefficient of 0.858 for MATH-500, 0.836 for AMC 2023
and 0.833 for AIME 2024, showing similar trends to the correlation
between the number of backtracks and the model’s performance
(Section [4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 Impact of the Search Prior ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ ASTRO: Teaching Language Models to Reason by Reflecting and Backtracking In-Context")).

![Refer to
caption](2507.00417v1/astro_num_generated_tokens_eval_scores_v2.png)

Figure 17: Relationship between the number of generated tokens and
evaluation metrics on MATH-500, AMC 2023 and AIME 2024. There is
positive correlation between the number of generated tokens and
performance on the math benchmarks, indicating that the policy returns
more accurate answers as it generates more tokens during inference. The
Pearson’s coefficients are 0.858 0.836 and 0.833 for MATH-500, AMC 2023
and AIME 2024, respectively.

## Appendix D Details for Llama-3.1-70B-Direct-RL

We provide more details of Llama-3.1-70B-Direct-RL trained according to
our experimental setup described in
Section [4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 Impact of the Search Prior ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ ASTRO: Teaching Language Models to Reason by Reflecting and Backtracking In-Context").
Note that this model does not have any self-reflection or backtracking
priors infused during the SFT stage, as we seek to isolate the effects
of the search priors used in Astro.

### D.1 Training

Our training setups for the SFT and RL stages are identical to that of
training Llama-3.1-70B-ASTRO-SFT and Llama-3.1-70B-ASTRO-RL,
respectively. We focus on the RL portion of training
Llama-3.1-70B-Direct-RL and share further useful details regarding the
model’s training.

#### CoT generation length.

In
Figure [18](#A4.F18 "Figure 18 ‣ CoT generation length. ‣ D.1 Training ‣ Appendix D Details for Llama-3.1-70B-Direct-RL ‣ ASTRO: Teaching Language Models to Reason by Reflecting and Backtracking In-Context")
we show how the length of the CoT generated by Llama-3.1-70B-Direct-RL
evolves during RL. Without the self-reflection and backtracking priors,
we observe that the number of tokens of the policy’s generated CoT
increases more slowly, although it does show an increase from about 1K
tokens on average to about 2K tokens.

![Refer to caption](2507.00417v1/astro_direct_cot_generation_length.png)

Figure 18: The number of generated tokens on training prompts while
training Llama-3.1-70B-Direct-RL via RL.

## Appendix E Qualitative Examples

We include qualitative examples of chain-of-thoughts generated by
different models trained using Astro in our experiments for a better
understanding of the model behavior.

### E.1 ASTRO-SFT

Llama-3.1-70B-ASTRO-SFT is already able to perform autoregressive search
(self-reflections and backtracks), averaging about 1.2 tokens and 0.8
backtracks for MATH-500 and 3K tokens and 1.1 backtracks for AIME 2024.
The model explores over a wide solution space, generating both correct
and incorrect solution traces until it converges to the final answer
with high confidence and terminates its search process.
````
